newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 5.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- COMPUTER DATE 'BOMB' DANGERS ARE BIGGER THAN THOUGHT

Experts have warned that the potential damage from the so- called 'millennium bomb', where computer software is unable to cope with the date change from 1999 to 2000, has been greatly underestimated. In a letter to the Financial Times newspaper, Robin Guenier, head of Taskforce 2000 - the body set up by the government to tackle the problem - warns that "the problem is present in countless logic chips embedded in a multitude of devices from security and telephone systems to processing and power generation plant".
-- RESCUER OF LOTUS CARS DIES IN HELICOPTER CRASH

The Malaysian businessman who last year took over the ailing UK sports car and engineering business Lotus Group, has died in a helicopter crash. Yahaya Ahmad controlled Malaysia's national car group Proton, and had taken a 16.3 per cent personal stake in Lotus. Proton had planned substantial expansion for Lotus, and executives at the Norfolk-based company said that investment and recruitment at Lotus would not be affected by the tragedy.
-- PRISM TO SPEND 200 MILLION STG ON LTS LINE TRAINS

Prism Rail, the privatised rail operator which runs services on the notorious London, Tilbury & Southend (LTS) line, is to invest 200 million stg on 44 new air-conditioned trains for the service. The LTS line was once dubbed 'the misery line' because of its unreliability. The provisional contract for the new trains - the first significant such order since the break-up of British Rail - has been awarded to Adtranz (ABB Daimler-Benz).
-- MOVES TO CURB BT LEAD URGED

National Utility Services, the agency which provides cost control services to the telecoms, water and energy industries, has published a review which urges that British Telecom be forced to set prices at a level which would give rival carriers a better opportunity to compete with the UK's dominant operator. The report claims that BT has been left in a dominant position via 'a legacy of misdirected pricing initiatives' by regulators.
-- FORD CONFIDENT ON HALEWOOD SUBSIDY

Jac Nasser, chairman of Ford Europe, has given the clearest indication yet that the future of the company's plant on Halewood, Merseyside is assured. In January, Ford announced the plant would not be producing the next generation Escort model, casting a shadow over the future of the whole plant. But speaking at the Geneva motor show Tuesday, Nasser said Ford was 'on track' in its efforts to secure sufficient state subsidy from the UK government to continue volume carmaking at the plant beyond 2000.
-- CALL TO REJECT GAS PRICE DISCOUNT

Ofgas, the regulator of the UK's gas industry, is likely to be asked to reject proposals from the former British Gas GAS.L supply arm Centrica to cut prices for consumers in the south west of England, the first area to enjoy gas competition. The call is expected to be made by new entrants to the gas market, who claim a price cut by Centrica would undermine the growth of competition, still in its embryonic stage.
-- DAIMLER BOOSTED BY 700 MILLION STG PROFITS FORECAST

German industrial group Daimler-Benz has said it expects 1996 profits of at least DM2 billion (700 million stg), on sales of around DM107 billion. Both figures would be above market forecasts. Speaking at the Geneva motor show, where Mercedes-Benz was unveiling its revolutionary new small car the A-class, Daimler board member Eckhard Cordes offered the clearest signal yet that the group is recovering well following record losses of Dm5.7 billion in 1995.
-- IRELAND MAY GAIN FROM UK EMU 'OPT-OUT'

The Republic of Ireland might expect to gain further inward investment if it opted to join European monetary union and the UK remained outside it, claims one of the country's biggest industrial groups. Don Godson, chief executive of the CRH building materials group, outlined the advantages of Ireland to companies wanting an English-speaking base in Europe, and said that a decision by the UK to stay out of the first phase of Emu might attact companies who wanted to operate inside the common currency, to locate in Ireland.
-- STERLING HITS SMITH & NEPHEW

Medical equipment group Smith & Nephew has reported a 1 per cent increase in 1996 pre-tax profits to 178.7 million stg, on sales up 4 per cent to 1.07 billion stg. However, the company also said that currency movements could be expected to hit results this year if sterling and the dollar remain as strong as they are now.
-- PEUGEOT-CITROEN CHIEF URGES VALUE FOR SHAREHOLDERS

Jacques Calvet, chairman of French automotive group Peugeot-Citroen, has called for greater emphasis on shareholder value at the group, and suggested that the company's turnaround is not being reflected in the share price. Speaking at the Geneva motor showm Calvet, who is expected to retire later this year, said: "we need to have a sharper vision of the interests of shareholders", although he ruled out any special measures to boost the share price such as spinning off non-core activities.
